Mastodon is a **free, open-source social network server** based on [ActivityPub](https://www.w3.org/TR/activitypub/) where users can follow friends and discover new ones. On Mastodon, users can publish anything they want: links, pictures, text, and video. All Mastodon servers are interoperable as a federated network (users on one server can seamlessly communicate with users from another one, including non-Mastodon software that implements ActivityPub!) ## Navigation - [Project homepage 🐘](https://joinmastodon.org) - [Donate to support development 🎁](https://joinmastodon.org/sponsors#donate) - [View sponsors](https://joinmastodon.org/sponsors) - [Blog 📰](https://blog.joinmastodon.org) - [Documentation 📚](https://docs.joinmastodon.org) - [Official container image 🚢](https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pkgs/container/mastodon) --- # Development ## Overview Before starting local development, read the [CONTRIBUTING] guide to understand what changes are desirable and what general processes to use. You should also read the project's [AI Contribution Policy] to understand how we approach AI-assisted contributions. ## Environments The following instructions will guide you through the process of setting up a local development instance of Mastodon on your computer. There are instructions for these environments: - [Vagrant](#vagrant) - [macOS](#macos) - [Linux](#linux) - [Docker](#docker) - [Dev Containers](#dev-containers) - [GitHub Codespaces](#github-codespaces) Once completed, continue with the [Next steps](#next-steps) section below. ### Vagrant A **Vagrant** configuration is included for development purposes. To use it, complete the following steps: - Install Vagrant and Virtualbox - Install the `vagrant-hostsupdater` plugin: `vagrant plugin install vagrant-hostsupdater` - Run `vagrant up` - Run `vagrant ssh -c "cd /vagrant && bin/dev"` - Open `http://mastodon.local` in your browser ### macOS To set up **macOS** for native development, complete the following steps: - Install [Homebrew] and run: `brew install postgresql@14 redis libidn nvm vips` to install the required project dependencies - Use a Ruby version manager to activate the ruby in `.ruby-version` and run `nvm use` to activate the node version from `.nvmrc` - Start the database services by running `brew services start postgresql` and `brew services start redis` - Run `RAILS_ENV=development bin/setup`, which will install the required ruby gems and node packages and prepare the database for local development (Note: If you are on Apple Silicon and get an error related to `libidn`, you should be able to fix this by running `gem install idn-ruby -- --with-idn-dir=$(brew --prefix libidn)`, then re-running the command above.) - Finally, run the `bin/dev` script which will launch services via `overmind` (if installed) or `foreman` ### Linux The Mastodon documentation has a [guide on installing Mastodon from source](https://docs.joinmastodon.org/dev/setup/#manual) on Linux. ### Docker For production hosting and deployment with **Docker**, use the `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` in the project root directory. For local development, install and launch [Docker], and run: ```shell docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml up -d docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/setup docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/dev ``` ### Dev Containers Within IDEs that support the [Development Containers] specification, start the "Mastodon on local machine" container from the editor. The necessary `docker compose` commands to build and setup the container should run automatically. For **Visual Studio Code** this requires installing the [Dev Container extension]. ### GitHub Codespaces [GitHub Codespaces] provides a web-based version of VS Code and a cloud hosted development environment configured with the software needed for this project. [![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)][codespace] - Click the button to create a new codespace, and confirm the options - Wait for the environment to build (takes a few minutes) - When the editor is ready, run `bin/dev` in the terminal - Wait for an _Open in Browser_ prompt. This will open Mastodon - On the _Ports_ tab "stream" setting change _Port visibility_ → _Public_ ## Next steps - Once you have successfully set up a development environment, it will be available on http://localhost:3000 - Log in as the default admin user with the username `admin@mastodon.local` or `admin@localhost` (depending on your setup) and the password `mastodonadmin`. - Check out the [Mastodon docs] for tips on working with emails in development (you'll need this when creating new user accounts) as well as a list of useful commands for testing and updating your dev instance. - You can optionally populate your database with sample data by running `bin/rails dev:populate_sample_data`. There are instructions for these environments: - [Vagrant](#vagrant) - [macOS](#macos) - [Linux](#linux) - [Docker](#docker) - [Dev Containers](#dev-containers) - [GitHub Codespaces](#github-codespaces) Once completed, continue with the [Next steps](#next-steps) section below. ### Vagrant A **Vagrant** configuration is included for development purposes. To use it, complete the following steps: - Install Vagrant and Virtualbox - Install the `vagrant-hostsupdater` plugin: `vagrant plugin install vagrant-hostsupdater` - Run `vagrant up` - Run `vagrant ssh -c "cd /vagrant && bin/dev"` - Open `http://mastodon.local` in your browser ### macOS To set up **macOS** for native development, complete the following steps: - Install [Homebrew] and run: `brew install postgresql@14 redis libidn nvm vips` to install the required project dependencies - Use a Ruby version manager to activate the ruby in `.ruby-version` and run `nvm use` to activate the node version from `.nvmrc` - Start the database services by running `brew services start postgresql` and `brew services start redis` - Run `RAILS_ENV=development bin/setup`, which will install the required ruby gems and node packages and prepare the database for local development (Note: If you are on Apple Silicon and get an error related to `libidn`, you should be able to fix this by running `gem install idn-ruby -- --with-idn-dir=$(brew --prefix libidn)`, then re-running the command above.) - Finally, run the `bin/dev` script which will launch services via `overmind` (if installed) or `foreman` ### Linux The Mastodon documentation has a [guide on installing Mastodon from source](https://docs.joinmastodon.org/dev/setup/#manual) on Linux. ### Docker For production hosting and deployment with **Docker**, use the `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` in the project root directory. For local development, install and launch [Docker], and run: ```shell docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml up -d docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/setup docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/dev ``` ### Dev Containers Within IDEs that support the [Development Containers] specification, start the "Mastodon on local machine" container from the editor. The necessary `docker compose` commands to build and setup the container should run automatically. For **Visual Studio Code** this requires installing the [Dev Container extension]. ### GitHub Codespaces [GitHub Codespaces] provides a web-based version of VS Code and a cloud hosted development environment configured with the software needed for this project. [![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)][codespace] - Click the button to create a new codespace, and confirm the options - Wait for the environment to build (takes a few minutes) - When the editor is ready, run `bin/dev` in the terminal - Wait for an _Open in Browser_ prompt. This will open Mastodon - On the _Ports_ tab "stream" setting change _Port visibility_ → _Public_ ## Next steps - Once you have successfully set up a development environment, it will be available on http://localhost:3000 - Log in as the default admin user with the username `admin@mastodon.local` or `admin@localhost` (depending on your setup) and the password `mastodonadmin`. - Check out the [Mastodon docs] for tips on working with emails in development (you'll need this when creating new user accounts) as well as a list of useful commands for testing and updating your dev instance. - You can optionally populate your database with sample data by running `bin/rails dev:populate_sample_data`. This will create a `@showcase_account` account with various types of contents. class StreamingServerManager
  @running_thread = nil

  def initialize
    at_exit { stop }
  end

  def start(port: 4020)
    return if @running_thread

    queue = Queue.new

    if ENV['DEBUG_STREAMING_SERVER'].present?
      logger = Logger.new($stdout)
      logger.level = 'debug'
    end

    @queue = queue

    @running_thread = Thread.new do
      Open3.popen2e(
        {
          'REDIS_DB' => (ENV.fetch('TEST_ENV_NUMBER', 0).to_i + 1).to_s,
          'DB_NAME' => "#{ENV.fetch('DB_NAME', 'mastodon')}_test#{ENV.fetch('TEST_ENV_NUMBER', '')}",
          'RAILS_ENV' => ENV.fetch('RAILS_ENV', 'test'),
          'NODE_ENV' => ENV.fetch('STREAMING_NODE_ENV', 'development'),
          'PORT' => port.to_s,
        },
        'node index.js', # must not call yarn here, otherwise it will fail because yarn does not send signals to its child process
        chdir: Rails.root.join('streaming')
      ) do |_stdin, stdout_err, process_thread|
        status = :starting

        # Spawn a thread to listen on streaming server output
        output_thread = Thread.new do
          stdout_err.each_line do |line|
            logger&.info "Streaming server: #{line}"

            if status == :starting && line.match('Streaming API now listening on')
              status = :started
              @queue.enq 'started'
            end
          end
        end

        # And another thread to listen on commands from the main thread
        loop do
          msg = queue.pop

          case msg
          when 'stop'
            # we need to properly stop the reading thread
            output_thread.kill

            # Then stop the node process
            Process.kill('KILL', process_thread.pid)

            # And we stop ourselves
            @running_thread.kill
          end
        end
      end
    end

    # wait for 10 seconds for the streaming server to start
    Timeout.timeout(10) do
      loop do
        break if @queue.pop == 'started'
      end
    end
  end

  def stop
    return unless @running_thread

    @queue.enq 'stop'

    # Wait for the thread to end
    @running_thread.join
  end
end

require 'concurrent/atomic/cyclic_barrier'

module ThreadingHelpers
  def multi_threaded_execution(thread_count)
    barrier = Concurrent::CyclicBarrier.new(thread_count)

    threads = Array.new(thread_count) do |index|
      Thread.new do
        barrier.wait
        yield(index)
      end
    end

    threads.each(&:join)
  end
end

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

require 'concurrent/atomic/cyclic_barrier'

module ThreadingHelpers
  def multi_threaded_execution(thread_count)
    barrier = Concurrent::CyclicBarrier.new(thread_count)

    threads = Array.new(thread_count) do |index|
      Thread.new do
        barrier.wait
        yield(index)
      end
    end

    threads.each(&:join)
  end
end

# frozen_string_literal: true

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end
end

messages.content: The median example takes 28 ms, and the fastest ones take about 1 ms, so the fixed hook overhead is small. The cost is in examples that touch the database, through factories, callbacks, and SQL. To locate it, I'll run one more profiled pass with StackProf (wall mode) plus SQL counters. The profiler lives in `/tmp`, so nothing in the repo changes.

arguments.command:
mkdir -p /tmp/perf && cat > /tmp/perf/profile_hook.rb <<'EOF'
# Temporary profiling hook (NOT part of repo). Loaded with `rspec -r`.
require 'stackprof'

$perf_sql = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [0, 0.0] }
$perf_sql_total = [0, 0.0]
$perf_example_sql = []

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.before(:suite) do
    ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe('sql.active_record') do |*args|
      ev = ActiveSupport::Notifications::Event.new(*args)
      next if ev.payload[:name] == 'SCHEMA'
      op = ev.payload[:sql].to_s.lstrip[/\A\w+/].to_s.upcase
      kind = ev.payload[:cached] ? "CACHED" : op
      $perf_sql[kind][0] += 1
      $perf_sql[kind][1] += ev.duration / 1000.0
      $perf_sql_total[0] += 1
      $perf_sql_total[1] += ev.duration / 1000.0
    end
    StackProf.start(mode: :wall, raw: true, interval: 1000)
  end

  config.after(:suite) do
    StackProf.stop
    StackProf.results('/tmp/perf/stackprof.dump')
    File.write('/tmp/perf/sql_stats.txt', (
      ["total queries=#{$perf_sql_total[0]} sql_time=#{$perf_sql_total[1].round(0)}ms"] +
      $perf_sql.sort_by { |_, v| -v[1] }.map { |k, v| format('%-12s count=%-8d time=%.0fms avg=%.3fms', k, v[0], v[1], v[1] / v[0]) }
    ).join("\n") + "\n")
  end
end
EOF
cd /app && (nohup bash -c 'start=$(date +%s); bundle exec rspec spec/models --seed 4242 -r /tmp/perf/profile_hook.rb --format progress > /tmp/perf/profile_models.log 2>&1; echo "DONE rc=$? secs=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" > /tmp/perf/profile_models.wall' >/dev/null 2>&1 &); echo started; date

messages.content: This is the key finding. About 35% of wall time sits under `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql`, mostly in `BacktraceCleaner` and `Thread.each_caller_location`. That means SQL debug logging is computing source locations for every one of the ~114k queries. The database itself accounts for only about 5 to 10%. I'll confirm the call path and the Rails version before deciding on a fix.

    def sql(event)
      payload = event.payload

      return if IGNORE_PAYLOAD_NAMES.include?(payload[:name])

      name = if payload[:async]
        "ASYNC #{payload[:name]} (#{payload[:lock_wait].round(1)}ms) (db time #{event.duration.round(1)}ms)"
      else
        "#{payload[:name]} (#{event.duration.round(1)}ms)"
      end
      name  = "CACHE #{name}" if payload[:cached]
      sql   = payload[:sql]
      binds = nil

      if payload[:binds]&.any?
        casted_params = type_casted_binds(payload[:type_casted_binds])

        binds = []
        payload[:binds].each_with_index do |attr, i|
          attribute_name = if attr.respond_to?(:name)
            attr.name
          elsif attr.respond_to?(:[]) && attr[i].respond_to?(:name)
            attr[i].name
          else
            nil
          end

          filtered_params = filter(attribute_name, casted_params[i])

          binds << render_bind(attr, filtered_params)
        end
        binds = binds.inspect
        binds.prepend("  ")
      end

      name = colorize_payload_name(name, payload[:name])
      sql  = color(sql, sql_color(sql), bold: true) if colorize_logging

      debug "  #{name}  #{sql}#{binds}"

cat > /tmp/perf/sql_templates_hook.rb <<'EOF'
# Temporary profiling hook (NOT part of repo): normalized SQL template counts.
$tpl = Hash.new(0)
$tpl_table = Hash.new(0)
$per_example = []
$cur_ex_queries = 0
RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.before(:suite) do
    ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe('sql.active_record') do |*args|
      ev = ActiveSupport::Notifications::Event.new(*args)
      next if ev.payload[:name] == 'SCHEMA'
      sql = ev.payload[:sql].to_s
      norm = sql.gsub(/'(?:[^']|'')*'/, '?').gsub(/\b\d+(\.\d+)?\b/, '?').gsub(/\$\d+/, '?').gsub(/\s+/, ' ').strip
      norm = norm[0, 260]
      $tpl[norm] += 1
      if (m = sql.match(/\A\s*(?:SELECT|INSERT INTO|UPDATE|DELETE FROM)\s+"?(\w+)"?/i))
        $tpl_table["#{m[0].split.first.upcase} #{m[1]}"] += 1
      end
      $cur_ex_queries += 1
    end
  end
  config.around(:each) do |ex|
    $cur_ex_queries = 0
    ex.run
    $per_example << [$cur_ex_queries, ex.metadata[:location]]
  end
  config.after(:suite) do
    out = []
    out << "== total templates: #{$tpl.size}, total queries: #{$tpl.values.sum}"
    out << "== per table/op (top 40):"
    $tpl_table.sort_by { |_, v| -v }.first(40).each { |k, v| out << format('%8d  %s', v, k) }
    out << "== top 40 SQL templates:"
    $tpl.sort_by { |_, v| -v }.first(40).each { |k, v| out << format('%8d  %s', v, k) }
    pe = $per_example.sort_by { |q, _| -q }
    out << "== examples with most queries (top 25):"
    pe.first(25).each { |q, loc| out << format('%6d  %s', q, loc) }
    out << "== queries per example: mean=%.1f median=%d" % [$per_example.sum { |q, _| q } / $per_example.size.to_f, $per_example.map(&:first).sort[$per_example.size / 2]]
    out << "== examples with 0 queries: #{$per_example.count { |q, _| q.zero? }}"
    File.write('/tmp/perf/sql_templates.txt', out.join("\n") + "\n")
  end
end
EOF

Mastodon's test env turns 2,847 user inserts into per-user BCrypt work, which is also app-level. I'll aggregate the profile's self-time by source file so I can separate app code, gems, Rails internals, and spec-support hooks.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > /tmp/perf/self_by_file.rb <<'EOF'
require 'stackprof'
data = Marshal.load(File.binread(ARGV[0]))
frames = data[:frames]
total = data[:samples].to_f
by_file = Hash.new(0)
by_frame = Hash.new(0)
frames.each do |_id, f|
  next if f[:samples].to_i.zero?
  file = f[:file].to_s
  bucket =
    case file
    when %r{/usr/local/bundle/gems/([^/]+)/} then "gem:#{$1.sub(/-\d[\d.]*\z/, '')}"
    when %r{/usr/local/bundle/gems/} then 'gem:other'
    when %r{^/app/spec/fabricators|fabrication} then 'FACTORIES(fabricators)'
    when %r{^/app/spec/(rails_helper|spec_helper)} then 'spec:helpers'
    when %r{^/app/spec/support} then 'spec:support'
    when %r{^/app/spec/} then 'spec:examples'
    when %r{^/app/app/models} then 'app:models'
    when %r{^/app/app/} then "app:#{file.split('/')[3]}"
    when %r{^/app/lib} then 'app:lib'
    when %r{^/app/config} then 'app:config'
    when %r{^/app/} then 'app:other'
    when %r{<internal:} then 'ruby:internal'
    when '' then 'C/unknown'
    else "other:#{file[0, 60]}"
    end
  by_file[bucket] += f[:samples]
  by_frame[[bucket, f[:name]]] += f[:samples]
end
puts "total samples: #{data[:samples]}"
puts "\n== self samples grouped by source (top 40)"
by_file.sort_by { |_, v| -v }.first(40).each { |k, v| printf("%6.2f%%  %s\n", 100 * v / total, k) }
puts "\n== top self frames inside SPEC code (examples/support/helpers) and app code"
by_frame.select { |(b, _), _| b.start_with?('spec:', 'app:', 'FACT') }.sort_by { |_, v| -v }.first(30).each { |(b, n), v| printf("%6.2f%%  %-22s %s\n", 100 * v / total, b, n) }
EOF

require 'stackprof'
data = Marshal.load(File.binread(ARGV[0]))

pats = [
  /reload_routes_unless_loaded/, /reload!/, /Rails::Application#reload/,
  /Rails.cache|MemoryStore|clear\b/, /RedisConnection|redis/i, /Resolv/, /WebMock|webmock/i,
  /Sidekiq/, /rspec-mocks|RSpec::Mocks/, /ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql/,
  /TransactionManager|begin_transaction|rollback_transaction|commit_transaction|SavepointTransaction/,
  /BCrypt/, /Fabricat/, /Setting\./, /UserRole/, /Logger::LogDevice#write|LogDevice/,
  /Devise/, /Paperclip|Kt::Paperclip|kt-paperclip/, /Vips/, /ActiveRecord::Base.*(save|create)/
]
seen = {}
data[:frames].each do |_id, f|
  name = f[:name].to_s
  pats.each_with_index do |re, i|
    next unless name =~ re
    key = [i, name, f[:file].to_s.sub('/usr/local/bundle/gems/', '')]
    seen[key] ||= [0, 0]
    seen[key][0] += f[:total_samples].to_i
    seen[key][1] += f[:samples].to_i
  end
end
seen.sort_by { |_, v| -v[0] }.first(45).each do |(_, name, file), (tot, selfs)|
  printf("incl %6.2f%%  self %6.2f%%  %-60s %s\n", 100 * tot / total, 100 * selfs / total, name[0, 60], file[0, 60])
end
EOF

# frozen_string_literal: true

# WebhookService serializes the whole event payload before it looks up which
# enabled webhooks subscribe to the event. Specs create many local statuses and
# accounts without any webhook, where that payload is computed and then thrown
# away. Skip the serialization only when no enabled webhook subscribes to the
# event: the subscriber lookup still runs and the enqueued jobs (and so the
# observable behaviour) are unchanged. This is test-only; the production code is
# not modified.
#
# Enabled per example for `type: :model` (see the around hook below).
module SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization
  class << self
    attr_accessor :enabled
  end

  private

  def webhooks_for_event
    return super unless SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization.enabled

    @webhooks_for_event ||= super
  end

  def serialize_event
    return super unless SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization.enabled
    return super if webhooks_for_event.any?

    nil
  end
end

WebhookService.prepend(SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization)

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.around(:each, type: :model) do |example|
    SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization.enabled = true
    example.run
  ensure
    SkipUnsubscribedWebhookSerialization.enabled = false
  end
end
EOF

To get defensible numbers I'll take paired measurements: two pristine runs and two current runs, interleaved, with the same seed. To run pristine code without leaving the working tree in a bad state, I'll use `git stash push -u` (which also stashes the new support file) and restore it in the same script. I'll check the stash list afterwards.

arguments.command:
cd /app && git status --short && cat > /tmp/perf/paired.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Interleaved paired measurements: pristine (HEAD, via stash) vs current working tree.
cd /app
run() { # $1 label
  local start=$(date +%s)
  bundle exec rspec spec/models --seed 4242 --format progress --format json --out /tmp/perf/paired_$1.json > /tmp/perf/paired_$1.log 2>&1
  echo "$1 rc=$? secs=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" >> /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt
}
for round in 1 2; do
  git stash push -u -m "perf-phase1-current" >> /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt 2>&1
  run pristine_$round
  git stash pop >> /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt 2>&1
  run current_$round
done
echo ALLDONE >> /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/perf/paired.sh && rm -f /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt && (nohup /tmp/perf/paired.sh > /tmp/perf/paired_driver.log 2>&1 &) ; sleep 5; cat /tmp/perf/paired_status.txt; git stash list

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > docs/rspec-performance.md <<'EOF'
# RSpec suite performance: notes, baselines and plan

Living document for the "make the suite fast again" effort. Update the
numbers and the phase log whenever a change is measured.

- Goal: the full RSpec run (serial, no parallelisation) on CI had grown past
  10 minutes.
- Phase 1: `spec/models`. Target: at least 30-35% faster. **Done: about 61%
  faster** (see results).
- Phase 2: `spec/requests`. Then the combined target: `spec/models` +
  `spec/requests` at least 2x faster than the baseline (see "Phase 2 plan").
- Constraints that applied in every phase: no app code changes that alter
  runtime behaviour, no changes to what examples assert, factories untouched
  until their own phase, system and streaming specs ignored.

## How to measure

```bash
cd /app
bundle exec rspec spec/models --seed 4242 --format progress --format json --out tmp/perf/models.json
```

- Always pass a fixed `--seed`. `config.order = 'random'` makes the order
  (and therefore the cost of shared state) differ otherwise.
- Read the timing from the JSON: `summary.duration` is the sum of example time
  and matches wall-clock minus about 2-3 s of boot. Do not use the console
  "Finished in" line for comparisons.
- Run one `rspec` process at a time. Runs share the `mastodon_test` database
  and the Redis keyspace (`config.after` flushes Redis keys), so concurrent runs
  corrupt each other.
- This container is noisy: the same code and seed varied by about 10-20%
  between runs (models: 48.0 s and 58.4 s; requests: 135 s and 173 s). For any
  claim, interleave a pristine run and a changed run (see "Paired runs").
- `log/test.log` grows by about 100 MB per models run at debug level. After the
  phase 1 log-level change it stays small by default. Truncate it when needed.
- Tools that are not on this box: `python3`, `bc`. Use Ruby for JSON analysis.

Environment during the measurements (container, shared VM host):

## Phase 1 (spec/models): what was wrong and what changed

Three shared problems explained nearly all of the models overhead. Shares below
are from StackProf sample counts on the same seed.

### 1. A spec leaked `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` into the whole run

`spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` assigned the global
at load time (in the `describe` body), so it was in effect for every example in
the process. With verbose query logs on, ActiveRecord computes the caller
source location of every SQL query by walking the backtrace
(`ActiveSupport::BacktraceCleaner#first_clean_frame` and
`Thread.each_caller_location`). That was about 30% of all samples.

Fix: scope the setting to that group with an `around` hook that restores the
previous value. The spec's assertions are unchanged.

Rule for future specs: never assign global configuration in a `describe` body
or at file load time. Use an `around` hook that restores the old value.

### 2. Every local status, account, report and user event serialized its webhook payload for nothing

`WebhookService#call` builds the full ActiveModelSerializers payload
(`serialize_event`) before it asks which enabled webhooks subscribe to the
event. Specs create lots of local records with no webhook configured, so the
payload was computed and thrown away. Serialization alone was about 24.5% of
samples and about 35k of the roughly 114k SQL queries per run (serializers load
`account_stats`, `user_roles`, `user_ips`, `user_invite_requests`, ...).

Fix (test-only, `spec/support/skip_unsubscribed_webhook_serialization.rb`): a
prepended module skips `serialize_event` when no enabled webhook subscribes to
the event. The subscriber lookup still runs, so the enqueued delivery jobs and
the return value are unchanged. The shortcut is switched on by an `around`
hook for `type: :model` only, so other spec types are not affected in this
phase. Its own check (not committed) covered: no subscriber means no
serialization and no enqueue; an enabled subscriber still serializes and
enqueues; a disabled subscriber counts as no subscriber.

The production code has the same waste: `WebhookService` serializes for every
local event on every instance, whether or not a webhook exists. Reordering the
check in app code would fix it at the source. That is an app change, so it was
deliberately not made in this phase. It needs a decision from the owners.

### 3. Debug-level test logging formatted every SQL query

Rails' default test log level is `debug`. Each SQL query then builds a debug
message (name, binds, colorised SQL) and writes it to `log/test.log`. That was
about 8.4% of samples plus about 1.6% for the logger writes, and about 90-100 MB
of log per models run.

Fix: `config/environments/test.rb` sets `config.log_level =
ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'info')`. Set `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug` to get SQL
logs back when debugging a spec. Nothing in the suite asserts on debug output:
the only logger assertion stubs `Rails.logger.debug`, and `httplog` is still
loaded in the test env.

## Profile after phase 1 (spec/models, sample shares)

- Factory creation (`Fabrication::Generator`, `Fabricate`): about 80% inclusive
  (most of it is ActiveRecord save callbacks).
- ActiveRecord internals: about 24% self. ActiveModel validations: about 7%
  self. ActiveSupport callbacks: about 7% self.
- PostgreSQL round trips (`exec*`, `IO.select`): about 24%. About 79k queries
  per run, about 44 per example on average (median 21).
- Paperclip post-processing (thumbnails, image and audio processing): about 9%
  inclusive.
- BCrypt password hashing: about 7% inclusive. Devise sets `stretches = 1` in
  test, but bcrypt clamps the cost to its minimum of 4, so each fabricated user
  costs about 1.1 ms.
- GC: about 5%.
- Remaining webhook overhead (subscriber lookup, `TriggerWebhookWorker#find`):
  about 4%.

Top remaining SQL templates per run:

- `SELECT user_roles WHERE id = ?` (about 5.8k): `belongs_to :role` loads the
  role again for each user instance.
- `username_blocks` existence check (about 5.7k): one per account validation.
- `SAVEPOINT` / `RELEASE` (about 5.6k): from nested transactions in callbacks.
- `SELECT 1 AS one` uniqueness validations (about 26k): standard Rails
  validators.
- `SELECT webhooks ... ? = ANY(events)` (about 3.8k): the subscriber lookup
  that remains.
- `settings WHERE var = ?` (about 3k): settings are re-read because
  `Rails.cache.clear` runs after each example.

Heaviest examples by query count (candidates for per-example review in a
later phase): `trends/statuses_spec.rb:140` (1444 queries),

## Tried and rejected (measured or checked)

- YJIT (`RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1`): 51.2 s vs 48.0 s. Slower for a run this short
  (warm-up cost). Not recommended for this suite.
- RSA key generation: local accounts generate a 2048-bit key in
  `Account#generate_keys` (about 52 ms each). The account fabricator already
  supplies a keypair, so the cost does not occur in specs. Not a problem.
- `sleep` in specs: none in `spec/models`.
- `use_transactional_tests: false` and DatabaseCleaner: none in
  `spec/models`, so no cleanup cost.
- Redis cleanup in `config.after` (`redis.del(redis.keys)`) and
  `Rails.cache.clear`: negligible (the keyspace is empty between examples).
- Routes reload and DNS stubs in `config.before`: negligible in the profile.

## Phase 2 plan (spec/requests)

Target: together with models, at most about 150 s combined. With models at
about 50 s, requests need to come down to about 100 s from about 175 s, which is
about -43%.

1. Profile `spec/requests` the same way (the profile hook and the per-file

   controllers, signed requests (`SignedRequestHelpers`, RSA signing and
   verification), serializers, and Devise sign-in in request helpers.
2. Look at `cache_spec.rb` (258 examples, 35.6 s) first. It is the largest
   single file. Check whether its examples share setup that is rebuilt per
   example.
3. Shared examples in `spec/support/examples/api.rb` run 239 times. Check their

4. Extend the webhook skip to `type: :request` if the profile still shows

5. Keep checking for global state assigned at load time:

## Factories phase (later, not started)

- Paperclip post-processing for media attachments (about 9% of models samples):
  check which fabricators generate thumbnails or process real files, and

- BCrypt cost is a floor of 4 in bcrypt. Reducing it would mean changing the

- Account and user fabricators create extra records (a user per account, the

## App-level findings (reported, not changed)

These cost time in production as well as in tests. None is changed here, and
each needs a decision from the owners.

- `WebhookService#call` serializes before checking for subscribers. Check

- `User#role` and similar associations load `UserRole` by id once per user

messages.content:
Phase 1 is done: `spec/models` dropped from about 128 s to about 50 s in paired runs, a 61% reduction, which clears the 30–35% target. The changes are in the working tree, not committed.

**What I found and changed** (ranked by impact; profiling was StackProf in wall mode, plus SQL counters):

1. **A spec leaked global state.** `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` set `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at load time, so every SQL query in the whole run computed caller source locations. That was about 30% of samples. The setting is now scoped to that spec group with an `around` hook that restores the previous value. Assertions are unchanged. (134 s → 79 s in the single-run ladder.)
2. **Webhook payloads were serialized for nothing.** `WebhookService#call` serializes the full event before it checks for subscribers, and specs create many local records with no webhook. That was about 25% of samples and about 35k of 114k queries per run. I added a test-only shortcut in `spec/support/skip_unsubscribed_webhook_serialization.rb`. It skips serialization only when no enabled webhook subscribes, and it is enabled only for `type: :model`. The subscriber lookup still runs, so enqueued jobs and return values are unchanged. I checked this with a temporary spec covering no subscriber, an enabled subscriber, and a disabled subscriber. (79 s → 57 s.)
3. **Debug-level test logging.** Every SQL query was formatted and written to `log/test.log`, about 8–10% of samples. `config/environments/test.rb` now sets `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'info')`. Set `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug` to get SQL logs back. (57 s → 48 s.)

**Results (seed 4242, example time):**
- Models: 129.4 s and 127.3 s pristine, against 50.5 s and 49.9 s with the changes. Each of the 1795 examples passes in every run, and I also ran a second seed (98765).
- Requests: paired pristine 177.7 s against 173.3 s with the changes. That is within noise, so this phase gained nothing measurable there. The log level is global config, so it applies to requests too, but I'm not claiming a requests gain.
- Run-to-run noise on this shared VM is about ±10–20%, so the single-run ladder numbers are approximate. The paired numbers are the reference.

**Judgment calls to review:**
- The webhook fix is test-only. The production `WebhookService` does the same wasted serialization for every local event, so reordering the subscriber check in app code would fix it at the source.
